title: Festival-season cultural production leaves a payment-network signal distinct from attendance
source_unit: Office for National Statistics Economic activity and social change in the UK, real-time indicators: 17 September 2026
geography: United Kingdom, with Scotland compared with the rest of the UK; creative-arts payment flows and retail footfall

observations.period: August 2026 compared with July 2026; inter-organisation payments involving Scottish arts organisations

denominator.unit: month-on-month comparison of anonymised aggregated Bacs Direct Debit, Bacs Direct Credit, and Faster Payment flows; no population denominator

scotland_arts_org_payments_to_other_uk_a.unit: percent increase in payment value from Scottish arts organisations to other UK arts organisations

rest_of_uk_equivalent_arts_org_payments.unit: percent change in equivalent payments in the rest of the UK

festival_signal.value: Scottish arts-organisation payments to other UK arts organisations have shown an August peak every year from 2021 to 2025, with August values 1.9 to 2.6 times the average of the other months in the year

mechanism.value: Festival-season cultural production can be observed as inter-organisation payment activity and geographic network concentration before it is interpreted as audience attendance or consumer spending

observations.method: ONS real-time indicator using anonymised and aggregated Bacs Direct Debit, Bacs Direct Credit, and Faster Payment System flows between organisations classified in SIC Division 90, comparing Scottish arts organisations with the rest of the UK.
observations.uncertainty: The indicator is an experimental official statistic in development. It excludes ticket sales and visitor spending, may contain SIC misclassification and fuzzy-matching false positives, excludes suppressed cells and unassigned regions, and does not measure jobs, artist income, audience size, or festival quality.
observations.subgroup: Arts organisations in Scotland and the rest of the UK whose inter-organisation payment flows are captured and regionally attributed.
observations.counterinterpretation: The August change may reflect payment timing, invoicing, one-off contracts, festival logistics, or classification artifacts rather than a broad expansion of cultural production; payment value is not the same as realized cultural participation or welfare.

observations.period: August 2026 compared with July 2026 and August 2025; UK retail footfall

denominator.unit: retail-footfall index comparison; no unique-person denominator

uk_retail_footfall_month_on_month.unit: percent change in estimated UK retail footfall from July 2026

uk_retail_footfall_year_on_year.unit: percent change in estimated UK retail footfall from August 2025

regional_pattern.value: Compared with August 2025, footfall rose 14% in London and 3% in Scotland, while it fell 5% in the North East and 5% in Yorkshire and the Humber

mechanism.value: Place-based consumer presence can recover year-on-year while weakening month-on-month, creating a timing and geography layer for cultural venues, high streets, and festival-linked spending without identifying cultural attendance

observations.method: ONS real-time indicator based on BT Active Intelligence estimated UK retail footfall, reported as non-seasonally-adjusted month-on-month and year-on-year changes.
observations.uncertainty: The series excludes people who live and work in retail areas, counts visits rather than unique visitors, is not seasonally adjusted, and is affected by calendar variation; retail footfall is not a cultural-participation or household-spending measure.
observations.subgroup: Visitors to UK retail locations, with regional comparisons where data were available.
observations.counterinterpretation: Footfall can move differently from transaction value, cultural attendance, transport access, or local wellbeing; London and Scotland changes cannot be interpreted as general regional consumer welfare.

boundary: This record adds a near-real-time cultural-production and place-consumer layer using administrative payment flows and footfall. It does not establish ticket sales, attendance, visitor spending, artist income, jobs, cultural quality, consumer welfare, or causal effects of festivals or geography.
